title: AGI Ruin: A List of Lethalities
summary: LessWrong essay (Eliezer Yudkowsky, June 5, 2022) listing 43 reasons the author expects AGI alignment to fail on the current path. It defines the bar for 'alignment' minimally: not exact human values or provable alignment, but not killing literally everyone, achieved on the first critical try. Section A argues the problem must be solved at a dangerous capability level with no retries; Section B covers the distributional leap from safe training to dangerous deployment, outer versus inner alignment (optimizing a loss does not instill that loss as a goal; reward is not ground truth; human raters err systematically), capabilities generalizing further than alignment, corrigibility being anti-natural, the unworkability of CEV-style sovereigns and corrigible AGI, and limits of interpretability and behavioral inspection; Section C criticizes the state of the AI safety field.
setting: Argumentative essay; no experiments; human evolution used as the main analogy for inner misalignment.

quotes.quote: When I say that alignment is difficult, I mean that in practice, using the techniques we actually have, "please don't disassemble literally everyone with probability roughly 1" is an overly large ask that we are not on course to get.
Trolley problems are not an interesting subproblem in all of this; if there are any survivors, you solved alignment.

We need to get alignment right on the 'first critical try' at operating at a 'dangerous' level of intelligence, where unaligned operation at a dangerous level of intelligence kills everybody on Earth and then we don't get to try again.

Even if you train really hard on an exact loss function, that doesn't thereby create an explicit internal representation of the loss function inside an AI that then continues to pursue that exact loss function in distribution-shifted environments.

This is a problem when you're trying to generalize out of the original training distribution, because, eg, the outer behaviors you see could have been produced by an inner-misaligned system that is deliberately producing outer behaviors that will fool you.
Human raters make systematic errors - regular, compactly describable, predictable errors.
Therefore, capabilities generalize further out-of-distribution than alignment, once they start to generalize at all.
Corrigibility is anti-natural to consequentialist reasoning; "you can't bring the coffee if you're dead" for almost every kind of coffee.

When you explicitly optimize against a detector of unaligned thoughts, you're partially optimizing for more aligned thoughts, and partially optimizing for unaligned thoughts that are harder to detect.

A strategically aware intelligence can choose its visible outputs to have the consequence of deceiving you, including about such matters as whether the intelligence has acquired strategic awareness; you can't rely on behavioral inspection to determine facts about an AI which that AI might want to deceive you about.
It's guaranteed that some of my analysis is mistaken, though not necessarily in a hopeful direction.

key_numbers.claim: Acceptable risk threshold stated for a pivotal task
key_numbers.quote: if you can get a powerful AGI that carries out some pivotal superhuman engineering task, with a less than fifty percent change of killing more than one billion people, I'll take it.

limitations_stated: The author calls the list poorly organized and says some of the analysis is guaranteed to be mistaken; none of the difficulties is claimed to be impossible in principle, only not solvable in time on the first critical try.
open_questions: How to get inner properties (not just outer behaviors) into a system; how to verify alignment when behavioral inspection can be deceived; whether any 'pivotal weak act' exists (the author argues none does).
sense_of_alignment: Alignment as getting a powerful AGI to carry out a task without killing everyone ('if there are any survivors, you solved alignment'), with outer alignment (the loss) and inner alignment (the goals actually learned) as distinct problems.
